MUQATIL:40:55-57/r1.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:40:55-57/r1.speaker: author
MUQATIL:40:55-57/r1.claim: Meccans mockingly ask when the promised punishment will arrive; God consoles the Prophet and says it will come as killing at Badr, angels striking faces and backs, and souls sent quickly to the Fire.

MUQATIL:40:55-57/r2.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:40:55-57/r2.speaker: author
MUQATIL:40:55-57/r2.claim: Tasbih means praying by God's command at dawn and in the afternoon, specifically the dawn and afternoon prayers.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p182#5/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p182#5/r1.speaker: قتادة
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p182#5/r1.claim: Qatada identifies evening and morning as Asr and Fajr, and says Quranic glorification refers to prayer.

TAB-FULL:v20p348/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v20p348/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v20p348/r1.claim: The Prophet must patiently carry out his mission, deliver revelation, and trust God's certain promise to give victory to him and the believers over those who deny the message.

TAB-FULL:v20p348/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v20p348/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v20p348/r2.claim: “Glorify your Lord with praise” means pray while thanking him; evening runs from solar decline to night, and morning from the second dawn to sunrise, though some extend morning into the rising sun and forenoon.

TAB-FULL:v20p348/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v20p348/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v20p348/r3.claim: The familiar Arab meaning of morning is the interval from the second dawn until sunrise, not the broader period after sunrise into the forenoon.

TAB-FULL:v20p348/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v20p348/r4.speaker: بعض نحويي البصرة
TAB-FULL:v20p348/r4.claim: A Basran grammarian takes the coordinated phrases as “in the evening and in the morning,” since the preposition biʾ can mean fī.

TAB-FULL:v20p348/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v20p348/r5.speaker: بعض نحويي البصرة
TAB-FULL:v20p348/r5.claim: Another grammarian says the meaning is to pray with praise at these two times and in these two periods, with biʾ and fī distributed across both.

SULAMI:v2p211#3/r1.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v2p211#3/r1.speaker: بعضهم
SULAMI:v2p211#3/r1.claim: Patience in well-being is harder than seeking safety in a time of fear.

SULAMI:v2p211#3/r2.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v2p211#3/r2.speaker: النباحي
SULAMI:v2p211#3/r2.claim: Patience in obedience is motivated by fear of the afterlife.

SULAMI:v2p211#3/r3.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v2p211#3/r3.speaker: النباحي
SULAMI:v2p211#3/r3.claim: Patience is a fortress of truthfulness and a route to the afterlife; patience in obedience leads to the stations of the truthful and is a refuge of the Gentle.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:40:55-57/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:40:55-57/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:40:55-57/r1.claim: Muhammad should be patient because God's promise to aid him and destroy his enemies is true; glorifying with praise means praying gratefully at both ends of the day.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v7p152#2/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v7p152#2/r3.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v7p152#2/r3.claim: Muhammad should be patient through harm because God’s promise to establish his religion and destroy enemies is true; seeking forgiveness raises his rank and models worship.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v7p152#2/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v7p152#2/r4.speaker: الكلبي
BAGHAWI-FULL:v7p152#2/r4.claim: The fighting verse abrogated the patience verse.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v7p152#2/r5.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v7p152#2/r5.speaker: الحسن
BAGHAWI-FULL:v7p152#2/r5.claim: Evening and morning means ʿAṣr and Fajr; Ibn ʿAbbās says it means the five prayers.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p564/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p564/r3.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p564/r3.claim: Patience means waiting for fulfillment of God's promise, as Moses' outcome foreshadows Muhammad's; al-Kalbī says the fighting verse abrogated patience wherever it occurs.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p564/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p564/r4.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p564/r4.claim: Seeking forgiveness may have preceded God's later assurance of forgiveness, since this sūra is Meccan and al-Fatḥ is later; alternatively the command addresses the Prophet but intends his community.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p564/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p564/r5.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p564/r5.claim: Ibkār and bukr mean the same; al-Ṭabarī places ibkār from second dawn to sunrise, others from sunrise to midmorning, and al-Ḥasan takes evening and morning as ʿaṣr and dawn prayers.

TABRISI:40:51-55/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:40:51-55/r8.speaker: author
TABRISI:40:51-55/r8.claim: The Prophet is commanded to endure his people’s abuse because God’s promise of victory in this life and reward in the next is true; the reading treats seeking forgiveness as a command for a minor sin only if such sins are possible for prophets.

TABRISI:40:55/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:40:55/r1.speaker: author
TABRISI:40:55/r1.claim: The sound view is that seeking forgiveness is devotional: it raises the Prophet’s rank and establishes a practice for later believers, rather than implying a sin by him.

TABRISI:40:55/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:40:55/r2.speaker: author
TABRISI:40:55/r2.claim: Glorifying God with praise means declaring Him transcendent, thanking Him, attributing blessings to Him, and denying any likeness; another view purifies His attributes or deeds from created or unjust qualities.

TABRISI:40:55/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:40:55/r3.speaker: author
TABRISI:40:55/r3.claim: Another interpretation takes the command to glorify God as a command to pray.

TABRISI:40:55/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:40:55/r4.speaker: مجاهد
TABRISI:40:55/r4.claim: For Mujahid, al-ʿashī extends from the sun’s decline until night and al-ibkār from the second dawn until sunrise; Ibn Abbas instead identifies the five prayers.

TABRISI:40:55/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:40:55/r5.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
TABRISI:40:55/r5.claim: A prophetic report quotes God telling people to remember Him for an hour after morning and after afternoon, promising to take care of their concerns.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v7p232#3/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v7p232#3/r1.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v7p232#3/r1.claim: Be patient with their abuse because God's promise to grant victory is true; the chapter repeats this verse at 40:77.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v7p232#3/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v7p232#3/r2.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v7p232#3/r2.claim: Some say this command to endure was abrogated by the sword verse.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v7p232#3/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v7p232#3/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v7p232#3/r4.claim: One interpretation of the evening and morning prayers is the five daily prayers.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v7p232#3/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v7p232#3/r5.speaker: قتادة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v7p232#3/r5.claim: Another interpretation is the dawn and afternoon prayers.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v7p232#3/r6.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v7p232#3/r6.speaker: الحسن
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v7p232#3/r6.claim: A third view takes them as two cycles of prayer at dawn and dusk, performed before the obligatory prayers were instituted.

QURTUBI-FULL:40:55-56/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:40:55-56/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:40:55-56/r1.claim: The Prophet should patiently bear the polytheists' harm; God's promise of victory and vindication is true, as with Moses and the Children of Israel.

QURTUBI-FULL:40:55-56/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:40:55-56/r10.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:40:55-56/r10.claim: Another reading urges continual praise in and outside prayer, keeping the Prophet occupied instead of hastening victory.

QURTUBI-FULL:40:55-56/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:40:55-56/r2.speaker: الكلبي
QURTUBI-FULL:40:55-56/r2.claim: Al-Kalbī says this command to be patient was abrogated by the sword verse.

QURTUBI-FULL:40:55-56/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:40:55-56/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:40:55-56/r3.claim: One interpretation takes the sin to be the community's sin, with the possessed noun omitted.

QURTUBI-FULL:40:55-56/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:40:55-56/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:40:55-56/r4.claim: If prophets may commit minor sins, the request can refer to the Prophet's own sin.

QURTUBI-FULL:40:55-56/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:40:55-56/r5.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:40:55-56/r5.claim: Those who deny minor sins explain the command as devotional prayer, increasing the Prophet's rank and establishing a practice for later people.

QURTUBI-FULL:40:55-56/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:40:55-56/r6.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:40:55-56/r6.claim: A further interpretation is that forgiveness concerns a sin committed before prophethood.

QURTUBI-FULL:40:55-56/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:40:55-56/r7.speaker: الحسن وقتادة
QURTUBI-FULL:40:55-56/r7.claim: They interpret glorification in evening and morning as the Fajr and ʿAṣr prayers.

QURTUBI-FULL:40:55-56/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:40:55-56/r8.speaker: الماوردي
QURTUBI-FULL:40:55-56/r8.claim: Another view says these were two dawn and two evening rakʿahs performed in Mecca before the five prayers were prescribed; Qurtubi says this may have been abrogated.

QURTUBI-FULL:40:55-56/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:40:55-56/r9.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:40:55-56/r9.claim: Tasbīḥ with praise means gratitude to God and praising Him.

BAYDAWI-FULL:40:52-55/r6.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:40:52-55/r6.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:40:52-55/r6.claim: The Prophet should endure polytheist abuse: God’s promise of victory is true, as Moses’ experience with Pharaoh demonstrates.

BAYDAWI-FULL:40:52-55/r7.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:40:52-55/r7.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:40:52-55/r7.claim: Seeking forgiveness means attending to religion and repairing lapses by leaving what was less fitting; God will suffice the Prophet by granting victory and making the matter manifest.

BAYDAWI-FULL:40:52-55/r8.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:40:52-55/r8.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:40:52-55/r8.claim: The evening and morning praise may mean continual glorification and thanksgiving, or prayer at those two times; in Mecca the obligation was two rakʿas morning and evening.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p77#8/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p77#8/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p77#8/r1.claim: Be patient with the bitter insults of your people; God's promise to support you and exalt your word is true.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p77#8/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p77#8/r2.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p77#8/r2.claim: “Seek forgiveness for your sin” means the sin of your community.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p77#8/r3.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p77#8/r3.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p77#8/r3.claim: The evening and morning may mean the ʿAṣr and Fajr prayers, or repeating “Glory be to God and praise belongs to Him.”

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v9p266/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v9p266/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v9p266/r1.claim: The command to be patient is grounded in the earlier promise that God will help the messengers, so the Prophet must prevail over his enemies.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v9p266/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v9p266/r2.speaker: الكلبي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v9p266/r2.claim: Al-Kalbi says the patience command was abrogated by the sword verse.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v9p266/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v9p266/r3.speaker: ابن عطية
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v9p266/r3.claim: Ibn Atiyya says seeking forgiveness may predate the later revelation that past and future sins were forgiven, or address the Prophet while teaching others all the more to comply.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v9p266/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v9p266/r4.speaker: أبو عبد الله الرازي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v9p266/r4.claim: Al-Razi interprets the command as repentance for leaving what was more excellent and preferable.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v9p266/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v9p266/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v9p266/r5.claim: Other explanations make seeking forgiveness pure worship even when the requested outcome is guaranteed, or forgiveness for the community's sin against the Prophet.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v9p266/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v9p266/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v9p266/r6.claim: The two times named for glorification are hours when people attend to important work, but may instead stand for all times.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v9p266/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v9p266/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v9p266/r7.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies the morning and evening glorification with the five daily prayers.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v9p266/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v9p266/r8.speaker: قتادة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v9p266/r8.claim: Qatada identifies the times with the dawn and afternoon prayers.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v9p266/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v9p266/r9.speaker: الحسن
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v9p266/r9.claim: Al-Hasan first says they are two cycles of prayer before prayer became obligatory, and elsewhere identifies them as the afternoon and dawn prayers.

SAMIN-DURR:40:55/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:40:55/r1.speaker: قيل
SAMIN-DURR:40:55/r1.claim: لذنبك may be an objective verbal noun, meaning the sin of your community against you.

SAMIN-DURR:40:55/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:40:55/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:40:55/r2.claim: The apparent wording is that God says what He intends, even if humans may not ascribe a sin to the Prophet.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v7p151#3/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v7p151#3/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v7p151#3/r1.claim: The Prophet is told to be patient because God's promise to raise his message and give him and his followers the final outcome is true and unfailing.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v7p151#3/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v7p151#3/r2.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v7p151#3/r2.claim: The command to seek forgiveness urges the wider community to seek forgiveness; evening and early morning name the late day/early night and the start of day/late night.

BIQAI-FULL:v6p524#2/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v6p524#2/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v6p524#2/r1.claim: The promise to aid the messengers stands despite their enemies' threats, just as God gave guidance and scripture to Moses and granted him the eventual victory over Pharaoh.

BIQAI-FULL:v6p524#2/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v6p524#2/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v6p524#2/r2.claim: The Prophet should endure their abuse because God brings events about in their proper settings through the causes established for this world.

BIQAI-FULL:v6p524#2/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v6p524#2/r3.speaker: القشيري
BIQAI-FULL:v6p524#2/r3.claim: Al-Qushayrī says patience while awaiting God's promise rises in proportion to a person's faith and certainty.

BIQAI-FULL:v6p524#2/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v6p524#2/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v6p524#2/r4.claim: Seeking forgiveness for the Prophet's “sin” means seeking forgiveness for every complete deed; he is already forgiven, and the wording teaches his community by example.

BIQAI-FULL:v6p524#2/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v6p524#2/r5.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v6p524#2/r5.claim: Calling a complete deed a sin follows the maxim that the good deeds of the righteous are faults for those brought near to God.

BIQAI-FULL:v6p524#2/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v6p524#2/r6.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v6p524#2/r6.claim: The command to glorify God affirms His perfection and negates every defect; ascent in knowledge makes the creature's limits clearer.

BIQAI-FULL:v6p524#2/r7.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v6p524#2/r7.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v6p524#2/r7.claim: Evening and morning cycles show the Creator's ability to restore what has perished, supporting the Resurrection.

BIQAI-FULL:v6p524#2/r8.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v6p524#2/r8.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v6p524#2/r8.claim: The verse urges the dawn and afternoon prayers, which angels of night and day witness; Ibn ʿAbbās instead says it refers to all five prayers.

BURSEVI:v8p148#2/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v8p148#2/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v8p148#2/r1.claim: God’s promise includes victory, Islam’s supremacy over religions, and the conquest of Mecca and similar successes; it cannot fail, as the story of Moses and Pharaoh confirms.

BURSEVI:v8p148#2/r10.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v8p148#2/r10.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v8p148#2/r10.claim: The Prophet’s lapses of attention also differ from the ordinary forgetfulness known to his community.

BURSEVI:v8p148#2/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v8p148#2/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v8p148#2/r2.claim: Seeking forgiveness for the Prophet’s sin means remedying an occasional omission of the better, since God will suffice to make His religion prevail.

BURSEVI:v8p148#2/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v8p148#2/r3.speaker: عين المعاني
BURSEVI:v8p148#2/r3.claim: Ayn al-Ma‘ani phrases the matter conditionally: seek forgiveness for a sin, if one came from you.

BURSEVI:v8p148#2/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v8p148#2/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v8p148#2/r4.claim: Another view says the command is devotional instruction for the Messenger, raising his rank and establishing a practice for later believers.

BURSEVI:v8p148#2/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v8p148#2/r5.speaker: عرائس البقلي
BURSEVI:v8p148#2/r5.claim: ‘Ara’is al-Baqli calls the occurrence of the temporal in the eternal realm a sin.

BURSEVI:v8p148#2/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v8p148#2/r6.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v8p148#2/r6.claim: Another interpretation takes ‘your sin’ to mean the sin of the Prophet’s community.

BURSEVI:v8p148#2/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v8p148#2/r7.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v8p148#2/r7.claim: The community-only reading cannot explain the same wording when it adds a separate command to seek forgiveness for believing men and women.

BURSEVI:v8p148#2/r8.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v8p148#2/r8.speaker: ابن الشيخ
BURSEVI:v8p148#2/r8.claim: Ibn al-Shaykh says God means what He says, even though believers may not attribute a sin to the Prophet.

BURSEVI:v8p148#2/r9.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v8p148#2/r9.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v8p148#2/r9.claim: I strongly endorse Ibn al-Shaykh: prophethood exceeds sainthood, so no saint can know a prophet’s state or the reality of a sin attributed to him; only God knows it, like the secret of blessings on the Prophet.

BURSEVI:v8p148#3/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v8p148#3/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v8p148#3/r1.claim: Morning and evening glorification joined with praise means continuing it at all times, since the two terms together span the day.

BURSEVI:v8p148#3/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v8p148#3/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v8p148#3/r2.claim: Ishari reading: the sincere seeker’s heart should patiently endure the lower self, desire, and Satan; God’s promise of victory applies to the heart struggling against its unbelieving self.

BURSEVI:v8p148#3/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v8p148#3/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v8p148#3/r3.claim: The heart’s request for forgiveness means cleansing traits acquired from the lower self, which have clouded its mirror; obedience and remembrance polish away blameworthy character.

BURSEVI:v8p148#3/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v8p148#3/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v8p148#3/r4.claim: The body belongs to the visible realm and the heart to the unseen; effects flow from heart to limbs and also from bodily states back to the heart, so outward deeds repair and illuminate it.

BURSEVI:v8p148#3/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v8p148#3/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v8p148#3/r5.claim: Devotion should continue without slackness, inwardly or outwardly: pray while receptive, then recite, then remember with tongue and heart, then keep watchfulness if remembrance tires you; if thoughts overwhelm you, sleep.

BURSEVI:v8p148#3/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v8p148#3/r6.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v8p148#3/r6.claim: Muraqaba is the heart’s awareness that God sees it; this awareness itself is remembrance and its finest form.

ALUSI-FULL:v24p77#4/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v24p77#4/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v24p77#4/r1.claim: After the stories are given for consolation, the Prophet is told to endure the harm inflicted by the polytheists.

ALUSI-FULL:v24p77#4/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v24p77#4/r10.speaker: ابن عباس
ALUSI-FULL:v24p77#4/r10.claim: A report attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās takes the command as the five daily prayers when glorification means prayer.

ALUSI-FULL:v24p77#4/r11.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v24p77#4/r11.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v24p77#4/r11.claim: Those who dispute God's signs include those disputing His proofs of unity, revealed books, and miracles without a God-given proof; religious argument must rest on clear evidence.

ALUSI-FULL:v24p77#4/r12.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v24p77#4/r12.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v24p77#4/r12.claim: The rule applies to every false disputant, although the immediate occasion was, most likely, Meccan polytheists.

ALUSI-FULL:v24p77#4/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v24p77#4/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v24p77#4/r2.claim: God's promise to the Prophet and believers is victory, explicitly linked to the promise in 40:51; alternatively it includes all divine promises, especially victory.

ALUSI-FULL:v24p77#4/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v24p77#4/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v24p77#4/r3.claim: God never breaks His promise, so victory for the Prophet and believers must occur; the fates of Moses and Pharaoh provide an example.

ALUSI-FULL:v24p77#4/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v24p77#4/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v24p77#4/r4.claim: Seeking forgiveness means turning diligently to religious duties and repairing lapses that count as sins relative to the Prophet's rank, though not actual sins.

ALUSI-FULL:v24p77#4/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v24p77#4/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v24p77#4/r5.claim: Another view takes the sin as the community's sin against the Prophet, with the genitive construction understood as an objective relation.

ALUSI-FULL:v24p77#4/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v24p77#4/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v24p77#4/r6.claim: Mentioning evening and morning may mean persistence in glorification and praise throughout all times.

ALUSI-FULL:v24p77#4/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v24p77#4/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v24p77#4/r7.claim: Alternatively, the command can mean the two specified periods, with glorification in its literal sense or as prayer.

ALUSI-FULL:v24p77#4/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v24p77#4/r8.speaker: قتادة
ALUSI-FULL:v24p77#4/r8.claim: Qatāda interprets the two periods as the dawn and afternoon prayers.

ALUSI-FULL:v24p77#4/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v24p77#4/r9.speaker: الحسن
ALUSI-FULL:v24p77#4/r9.claim: Al-Ḥasan interprets them as two rakʿahs in the morning and two in the evening; the source discusses differing claims about what was obligatory in Mecca.

ELMALILI:40:53-55/r4.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:40:53-55/r4.speaker: author
ELMALILI:40:53-55/r4.claim: The Prophet should endure the polytheists' abuse and remain steadfast because God's promise of victory is true and certain.

ELMALILI:40:53-55/r5.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:40:53-55/r5.speaker: author
ELMALILI:40:53-55/r5.claim: Seeking forgiveness asks God to cover shortcomings that one failed to remedy.

ELMALILI:40:53-55/r6.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:40:53-55/r6.speaker: author
ELMALILI:40:53-55/r6.claim: Morning and evening means continually: maintain praise and glorification so neither heart nor tongue becomes heedless of remembrance.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v24p169/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v24p169/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v24p169/r1.claim: The account of Moses interrupts 40:51 before the command to be patient; deliverance from subjection into independent rule parallels the Muslims and hints that the Qur'an will endure in their community.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v24p169/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v24p169/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v24p169/r5.claim: The command to be patient follows from God's promise to support His messengers: the Prophet should know God supports him and the believers and should not weaken.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v24p170/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v24p170/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v24p170/r1.claim: Inna emphasizes the promise and serves a causal role in the command to be patient; God's promise of victory is true, so the Prophet should not hasten it.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v24p170/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v24p170/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v24p170/r2.claim: The promised victory came at Badr, the conquest of Mecca, Ḥunayn, and other campaigns; Uḥud's setback tested believers and warned against disobeying the Prophet's order to hold position, before the final outcome favored them.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v24p170/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v24p170/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v24p170/r3.claim: Forgiveness and glorification follow patience as signs of gratitude, indirectly showing victory is certain; the Prophet seeks continued protection and forgiveness as worship and proper conduct, while the community is all the more urged to do so.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v24p170/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v24p170/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v24p170/r4.claim: Evening and morning stand for all times: evening runs from late day into night, and ibkār is the morning's first part; glorification completes inner and outer gratitude.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v24p170/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v24p170/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v24p170/r5.claim: Unlike the command after victory in Sūrat al-Naṣr, this command includes patience because the Prophet is still awaiting promised victory; after victory, the focus is pure gratitude.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v24p75#4/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v24p75#4/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v24p75#4/r1.claim: Sūrat Ghāfir is Meccan by consensus, apart from a view attributed to al-Ḥasan that excludes this verse.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v24p75#4/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v24p75#4/r2.speaker: الحسن
IBNASHUR-FULL:v24p75#4/r2.claim: Al-Ḥasan thought the command to glorify God at evening and morning was revealed concerning the five prescribed prayers and their times, which he placed in Medina; in Mecca he believed only two untimed rakʿahs daily were required.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v24p75#4/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v24p75#4/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v24p75#4/r3.claim: Ibn ʿĀshūr rejects that view as resting on a weak premise: most scholars place the five prayers and their times in Mecca, and tasbīḥ can retain its ordinary sense of glorification rather than refer to ritual prayer.

TABATABAI:40:55-56/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:40:55-56/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:40:55-56/r1.claim: After recounting Moses' true mission, the opponents' false arguments, and God's victory, the verse tells Muhammad to endure because God's promise of victory is true.

TABATABAI:40:55-56/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:40:55-56/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:40:55-56/r2.claim: The command follows the earlier call to consider past peoples; endure the idolaters' harm and disputes because God will fulfill His promise.

TABATABAI:40:55-56/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:40:55-56/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:40:55-56/r3.claim: Asking forgiveness for the Prophet's sin does not imply violation of a binding command, since he is protected from such disobedience.

TABATABAI:40:55-56/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:40:55-56/r4.speaker: بعضهم
TABATABAI:40:55-56/r4.claim: Some interpret the sin as the sin of the Prophet's community, for which he was granted intercession.

TABATABAI:40:55-56/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:40:55-56/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:40:55-56/r5.claim: The Prophet's glorification with praise means declaring God free of defect while praising His beautiful acts and blessings, continually or each morning and evening.

TABATABAI:40:55-56/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:40:55-56/r6.speaker: بعضهم
TABATABAI:40:55-56/r6.claim: Some take evening and morning as the obligatory prayers of afternoon and dawn; the author objects that the verse is Medinan but all five prayers were prescribed in Mecca.

TABATABAI:40:55-56/r7.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:40:55-56/r7.speaker: author
TABATABAI:40:55-56/r7.claim: Reliable reports, including the Ascension accounts, say the five daily prayers were prescribed together in Mecca, before any two-prayer reading could fit this Medinan verse.

ASAD-NOTES:40:53#n38/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:40:53#n38/r1.speaker: all classical commentators
ASAD-NOTES:40:53#n38/r1.claim: The passage first addresses the Prophet and, through him, every believer; Asad points to his note on 24:31 for the Prophet's own case.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-7-english:p12/r5.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-7-english:p12/r5.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-7-english:p12/r5.claim: The Moses–Pharaoh account warns Quraysh, encourages Muhammad and his companions to endure trials until victory, and profiles a Pharaoh’s family believer as a lesson for Quraysh and hesitant sympathizers.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-7-english:p26/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-7-english:p26/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-7-english:p26/r2.claim: The Moses and Pharaoh story supports the prior claim that a people rejecting their messenger are destroyed despite worldly grandeur, and assures the Prophet and companions to persevere in their duty.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-7-english:p43/r5.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-7-english:p43/r5.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-7-english:p43/r5.claim: Verse 55 summarizes the argument and reassures Muhammad to continue preaching: the promise of success for messengers and their followers in this world and the Hereafter is certain.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-7-english:p43/r6.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-7-english:p43/r6.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-7-english:p43/r6.claim: Seeking forgiveness and glorifying God with praise morning and evening are the method for acquiring the patience required for the promise to materialize.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-7-english:p44/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-7-english:p44/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-7-english:p44/r1.claim: Prayer and seeking forgiveness cultivate patience; the address is to Muhammad as representative of his people, so its attribution of sin should be read in that context.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:40:55/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:40:55/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:40:55/r1.claim: God's promise is the assurance in verse 51 that He will help His messengers and believers.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:40:55/r2.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:40:55/r2.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:40:55/r2.claim: Revealed during Mecca's most difficult days, the passage assures Muhammad and his community that the promise will come true, as it did for Moses and his followers.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:40:55/r3.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:40:55/r3.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:40:55/r3.claim: The command to seek forgiveness predates the Fath promise of forgiveness; using it to date these surahs is invalid because the later Nasr surah also commands the Prophet to seek pardon.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:40:55/r4.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:40:55/r4.speaker: Müfessirler
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:40:55/r4.claim: Some say seeking forgiveness concerns the Prophet's pre-prophethood errors or addresses his community through him, since prophets are protected from sin.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:40:55/r5.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:40:55/r5.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:40:55/r5.claim: The Prophet should not be exempted from the command: repentance and seeking forgiveness are acts of worship, and he swore that he sought forgiveness seventy or one hundred times daily.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:40:55/r6.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:40:55/r6.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:40:55/r6.claim: Sound reports say the Prophet swore he sought forgiveness seventy or one hundred times each day.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:40:55/r7.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:40:55/r7.speaker: Müfessirler
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:40:55/r7.claim: Some interpret morning and evening glorification as the afternoon and dawn prayers, or as two prayer times before the five daily prayers became obligatory.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:40:55/r8.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:40:55/r8.speaker: İbn Âşûr
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:40:55/r8.claim: The verse is not about the obligation or times of prayer; as in Nasr, it simply commands praise, glorification, and seeking forgiveness.

STUDYQURAN:40:55/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:40:55/r1.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:40:55/r1.claim: The verse addresses Muhammad and counsels patience, implying he will triumph over his adversaries as Moses and earlier prophets did.

STUDYQURAN:40:55/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:40:55/r2.speaker: Ṭs
STUDYQURAN:40:55/r2.claim: The true promise may mean God's aid in this world and reward in the Hereafter.

STUDYQURAN:40:55/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:40:55/r3.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:40:55/r3.claim: Alternatively, the promise may refer specifically to the promise of aid in verses 51–52.

STUDYQURAN:40:55/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:40:55/r4.speaker: those who maintain that prophets do commit minor sins
STUDYQURAN:40:55/r4.claim: For those who hold that prophets can commit minor sins, asking forgiveness means repenting for those sins.

STUDYQURAN:40:55/r5.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:40:55/r5.speaker: majority of Muslims
STUDYQURAN:40:55/r5.claim: The majority hold prophets protected from sin; the command instead urges worship and supplication so God may raise Muhammad's rank and make his practice an example for later people.

STUDYQURAN:40:55/r6.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:40:55/r6.speaker: Bḍ
STUDYQURAN:40:55/r6.claim: Eventide and dawn mean sunset and the time before sunrise; before the five prayers were instituted in Mecca, two prayer cycles were required in each period.

STUDYQURAN:40:55/r7.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:40:55/r7.speaker: Q
STUDYQURAN:40:55/r7.claim: Another interpretation takes eventide and dawn as the night prayer, ʿishāʾ, and the morning prayer, fajr.

STUDYQURAN:40:intro/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:40:intro/r3.speaker: Other commentators
STUDYQURAN:40:intro/r3.claim: Others extend the Madinan classification to verse 55 as well.

STUDYQURAN:40:intro/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:40:intro/r4.speaker: Still other commentators
STUDYQURAN:40:intro/r4.claim: Still others classify only verse 55 as Madinan, interpreting its dawn and eventide praise as morning and sunset prayers, made obligatory only in the last Makkan years.

STUDYQURAN:40:intro/r9.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:40:intro/r9.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:40:intro/r9.claim: Divine aid to messengers ends with condemnation of those too arrogant to worship God, then transitions to God’s power over creation.
